provisions_triggered.name: Due Process / Law of the Land

case_law.method: v1.1.0 case-law rebuild: authorities selected per decision point, each opinion retrieved from CourtListener and read; holding and quote taken from the opinion text; independently re-verified before release. Previous keyword-matched Justia listings were removed.

key_cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
key_cases.holding: The Court held that before a State may irrevocably sever the rights of parents in their natural child, the Due Process Clause requires proof by at least clear and convincing evidence.
key_cases.relevance: It is the controlling federal standard of proof for termination of parental rights, mirrored in W. Va. Code § 49-4-604.
key_cases.quote: due process requires that the State support its allegations by at least clear and convincing evidence

key_cases.court: Supreme Court of Appeals of West Virginia
key_cases.holding: The Court held that a parent who validly relinquished her parental rights lost her status as a 'parent' and therefore lacked standing to move under W. Va. Code § 49-6-6 for modification of the child's disposition, because a final termination order completely severs the parent-child relationship.
key_cases.relevance: It fixes the legal consequence of termination, voluntary or involuntary, for any later attempt to undo it.
key_cases.quote: a final order terminating a person's parental rights, as the result of either an involuntary termination or a voluntary relinquishment of parental rights, completely severs the parent-child relationship

key_cases.court: Supreme Court of Appeals of West Virginia
key_cases.holding: Reversing the circuit court, the Court held that incarceration alone does not automatically terminate parental rights but the rights of an incarcerated parent may be terminated on a best-interests analysis, and that Rule 43's eighteen-month permanency deadline must be strictly followed.
key_cases.relevance: It is the controlling WV authority on terminating the rights of an incarcerated parent.
key_cases.quote: Thus while the mere fact that someone is incarcerated will not result in automatic termination of parental rights, the parental rights of an incarcerated person may be terminated

key_cases.court: Supreme Court of Appeals of West Virginia
key_cases.holding: Reversing the return of an abused infant to his mother, the Court held that parental rights may be terminated where clear and convincing evidence shows extensive physical abuse in the parents' custody and the perpetrator remains unidentified, and it set out the duties of guardians ad litem.
key_cases.relevance: It is the leading WV case terminating rights on unexplained serious physical abuse of a child in parental custody.
key_cases.quote: There is no reasonable likelihood that the conditions of abuse can be substantially corrected because the perpetrator of Jeffrey R.L.'s physical abuse has not been identified

key_cases.case_name: Lassiter v. Department of Social Services of Durham County
key_cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
key_cases.holding: The Court held the Constitution does not require appointment of counsel for indigent parents in every termination proceeding, leaving that decision to the trial court in the first instance subject to appellate review.
key_cases.relevance: It sets the federal constitutional floor for counsel at termination, above which West Virginia's statutory right to appointed counsel operates.
key_cases.quote: leave the decision whether due process calls for the appointment of counsel for indigent parents in termination proceedings to be answered in the first instance by the trial court

key_cases.court: Supreme Court of Appeals of West Virginia
key_cases.holding: Affirming termination of parental rights where an infant was allowed to reach near-starvation, the Court held that compelling circumstances justified denying an improvement period and that immediate termination, without first employing a less drastic intervening alternative, is more reasonable where the child is under the age of three.
key_cases.relevance: It is the foundational West Virginia termination standard, quoted as controlling in both Jeffrey R.L. and Charity H., permitting termination without intervening less restrictive alternatives and tying the permissible wait to the child's age and vulnerability.
key_cases.quote: where a child is under the age of three immediate termination without an intervening period employing a less drastic alternative is more reasonable than in other cases
